tagline: Locks, aqueduct arches and river roads trace the Erie Canal corridor
intro: The Mohawk Towpath Byway follows local, county and state roads beside the Mohawk River and Erie Canal between Schenectady and Waterford. FHWA lists this National Scenic Byway at 26.2 miles, allowing 40 minutes for the drive and a day or two for its communities and history. The agency highlights canal locks and bridges alongside surviving eighteenth- and nineteenth-century architecture. The byway organization describes a rural corridor interspersed with natural areas, with river views appearing along a meandering route through trees.

A grassroots effort to showcase this section of the Mohawk corridor led to state designation in 2003 and national designation in 2005. Its name recalls the mules that pulled canal boats from the towpath. At Cohoes, sixteen locks once took a day to pass; the 1831 Albany–Schenectady railway offered travelers a way to avoid that delay. The Waterford Flight, completed in 1915, gave boats a route from the Hudson to the Mohawk bypassing Cohoes Falls.

Begin in Schenectady, where the Stockade District borders the Mohawk. The route crosses the river at Aqueduct on NY 146, then follows Riverview Road southeast. At Crescent it divides: the southern branch crosses toward Cohoes, while the northern branch runs through Halfmoon. Both branches meet in Waterford, where the byway ends at Third and Broad streets.

moments.title: Stockade District
moments.text: The Stockade District’s name recalls a wooden enclosure, but its streets now hold houses with layers of later additions and embellishments. Twelve Dutch houses stood within the early stockade. After independence, the deteriorating enclosure was dismantled; only some mostly buried footings remain. The neighborhood later declined, and residents formed the Stockade Association in 1957 to protect its historical character. Five years later, their campaign secured a city ordinance creating New York’s first local historic district. More than forty houses are over two hundred years old. Riverside Park occupies the district’s shore along the Mohawk River.

moments.title: Rexford
moments.text: At Rexford, canal boats once crossed over the Mohawk River on an aqueduct. The arches visible from the NY 146 bridge supported the towpath, where animals hauled the boats. Most of the aqueduct was demolished in 1918 as the Barge Canal replaced the older canal. Other canal structures found new uses: the Schenectady Yacht Club occupies a former canal store and uses the remains of Lock 21 to move boats between its grounds and the river. Lock 21 dates to the canal enlargement of 1842, another remnant of the waterway’s successive rebuilding.
moments.notice: Surviving aqueduct arches once supported the canal towpath across the Mohawk.

moments.title: Cohoes Falls
moments.text: Cohoes Falls drops as much as 90 feet, presenting a barrier the Erie Canal had to bypass. The original canal ran through Cohoes; the Barge Canal opened in 1918 on a route through Waterford instead. The falls also supplied industrial power: a dam built in 1831 harnessed the river for the city’s textile mills. The amount of water over the ledge varies with river flow and diversions for canal locks, electricity generation and the city water supply. In dry summers, it dries out entirely. Low water exposes shale formations in the riverbed.
